paragraphs: AICrypto evaluates whether language models can do cryptography across several kinds of work. Its tasks include 135 multiple-choice questions, 150 capture-the-flag challenges, and 30 proof problems. This combination tests remembered knowledge, practical vulnerability exploitation, and mathematical reasoning, allowing the evaluation to distinguish capabilities that a single question format could blur together.

Cryptography experts reviewed or constructed all tasks. For proofs, the benchmark supplies reference solutions and detailed scoring rules so that automated assessment can evaluate more than whether a final answer matches. The authors report high agreement between automated grading and human expert evaluations, and provide human expert baselines across every task type.

Testing 17 leading language models reveals uneven strengths. The strongest models match or exceed experts on cryptographic recall, common vulnerabilities, and routine proofs. They still struggle with abstract mathematics, reasoning across multiple steps, and dynamic analysis. These findings make the benchmark useful for separating strong performance on familiar cryptographic tasks from deeper reasoning abilities that remain challenging.
icml-2026-aicrypto-evaluating-cryptograp.tldr: AICrypto finds strong LLM performance on familiar cryptographic tasks but persistent difficulties with abstract mathematics and complex reasoning.

paragraphs: M-DESIGN tackles the cost of designing a neural network for a new task. Searching many architectures is expensive, while retrieving an existing model can leave useful improvements unexplored. The paper instead treats previous architectural edits and their measured performance effects as reusable evidence about how to improve a model.

The framework organizes this evidence into graphs and retrieves it while constructing sequences of fine-grained modifications. Its adaptive retrieval mechanism reassesses how well evidence from different source tasks transfers as refinement proceeds. For tasks outside the familiar distribution, predictive planners connect evidence across multiple steps to estimate potential gains. This reduces dependence on a repository already containing every useful design.

The evaluation uses a knowledge base containing 67,760 graph neural networks across 22 datasets. Under a strict search budget, M-DESIGN consistently beats the tested baselines and reaches the best performance available within the search space in 26 of 33 cases. The result supports reusing knowledge about architectural changes, beyond simply reusing completed models.
icml-2026-beyond-model-base-retrieval-we.tldr: M-DESIGN reuses evidence about architectural edits to guide efficient network refinement, reaching search-space best performance in 26 of 33 cases.

paragraphs: Converting natural-language questions into SQL often involves a workflow of reasoning and processing steps. This paper argues that committing to one workflow limits performance when queries differ substantially, especially on unusual or unfamiliar cases. It studies whether a system can construct a suitable workflow while answering each query, reducing the need for users to compare methods themselves.

The theoretical and empirical analysis links the advantage of optimal dynamic policies to differences among candidate workflows. If workflows have different strengths across queries, adapting the choice can exploit that variation. The proposed SquRL framework trains a language model through reinforcement learning to make these construction decisions. It combines rule-based rewards with dynamic actor masking to broaden exploration and pseudo rewards to improve training efficiency.

On widely used Text-to-SQL benchmarks, learned dynamic workflows consistently outperform the best static workflow methods. Gains are especially pronounced for complex queries and queries outside the training distribution. The findings support query-dependent workflow construction as a way to use differing workflow strengths more effectively.
icml-2026-beyond-static-pipelines-learni.tldr: SquRL learns to construct query-specific Text-to-SQL workflows, improving especially on complex and out-of-distribution queries.

paragraphs: Graph-based retrieval can help a language model find connected information, but matching entities does not necessarily identify the relationships needed for a faithful answer. CausalRAG2 addresses this problem by explicitly representing causal relationships. The paper also targets information isolation: splitting a knowledge graph into modules can make reasoning across those boundaries difficult.

Its framework organizes knowledge hierarchically and introduces causal gating across modules. This design aims to suppress misleading correlations while supporting reasoning over large knowledge graphs. The central contribution is therefore a change in how retrieved knowledge is organized and connected, with causal relationships informing access across the hierarchy rather than remaining confined to local or single-document contexts.

The authors also introduce HolisQA, a benchmark intended to test holistic comprehension beyond matching entities. Across multiple datasets and evaluation metrics, CausalRAG2 consistently outperforms competitive graph-based retrieval baselines. These findings support explicit causal organization and cross-module connections as useful ingredients for the evaluated retrieval-and-reasoning tasks, while the framework also targets scalability.
icml-2026-causalrag2-hierarchical-causal.tldr: CausalRAG2 organizes graph-based retrieval around causal links across hierarchical modules, improving results across multiple evaluated datasets.

paragraphs: Forecasting several time-varying signals together requires deciding which signals should exchange information. Treating each variable independently can discard useful connections, while allowing broad interaction can introduce misleading relationships. Crisp addresses this trade-off by using compatibility between oscillatory patterns as the basis for deciding which variables interact.

The method examines signals in the frequency domain and derives spectral priors that define a changing network of permitted interactions. A differentiable, adaptive blocking mechanism sets attention weights for spectrally incompatible neighbors to exactly zero. This makes the restriction explicit rather than merely assigning those neighbors smaller weights. A separate spectral gate also filters each variable's features using its own frequency characteristics.

The two components operate at complementary levels: one controls information exchange between variables, and the other refines the information each variable carries. Experiments report significant improvements over more than 20 baselines. The findings support spectral compatibility as an effective interaction principle in the evaluated forecasting problems, rather than establishing it as a universal rule for all dependencies.
icml-2026-crisp-a-spectral-based-interac.tldr: Crisp improves multivariate forecasting by restricting information exchange to variables with compatible frequency patterns.

paragraphs: DADP addresses how a control policy can handle unfamiliar transition dynamics: changes in how an environment responds to actions. Its approach learns a representation of the domain and uses that information to guide action generation, with the aim of supporting adaptation without additional training in the new domain.

The authors identify a problem with learning domain representations through predictions based on context close to the current step. That context can mix stable information about the domain with temporary features of the ongoing dynamics. A policy conditioned on this mixture can be confused about which information describes the domain itself, constraining adaptation.

Their Lagged Context Dynamical Prediction method instead predicts future states using context from further in the past. Increasing this time gap filters out transient properties and separates stable domain information without supervision. DADP then incorporates the resulting representation into its diffusion generation process by biasing the prior distribution and changing the diffusion target.

Experiments spanning locomotion and manipulation report better performance and generalization than prior methods. These findings support the proposed combination of separating stable domain information and incorporating it directly into diffusion-based action generation on the evaluated benchmarks.
icml-2026-dadp-domain-adaptive-diffusion.tldr: DADP separates stable domain information from transient dynamics and injects it into a diffusion policy, improving adaptation to unfamiliar dynamics in locomotion and manipulation benchmarks.

paragraphs: Multi-hop questions do not all require the same reasoning structure. Some involve checking several independent facts, while others require a sequence in which one inference supplies information for the next. DTKG starts from this distinction and argues that a single processing strategy can be inefficient or ineffective across both kinds of question.

The framework first classifies the question using a language model prompted with a few examples. It then sends the question to a tailored reasoning branch. This design responds to complementary weaknesses identified in existing methods: language-model fact verification struggles with chained inference, while constructing knowledge-graph paths can create redundant work for independent fact checks. Cognitive theories motivate the separation between initial categorization and subsequent deliberate processing.

Experiments spanning six datasets report performance improvements ranging from 5.0% to 29.5%. The findings support selecting a reasoning structure according to the dependencies within a question. DTKG's contribution is the coordinated classification-and-branching pipeline, which lets different question types receive different forms of knowledge-graph-verified reasoning.
icml-2026-dtkg-dual-track-knowledge-grap.tldr: DTKG classifies multi-hop questions and routes them to reasoning branches suited to independent fact checks or sequential inference.

paragraphs: E-mem addresses a memory problem for language-model agents working across extended interactions: converting past experience into compressed structures can break the sequential connections needed for later reasoning. The paper proposes preserving episodic context and reconstructing relevant evidence when needed, with biological engrams serving as inspiration for the design.

The architecture assigns uncompressed memory contexts to multiple assistant agents and gives a central master agent responsibility for global planning. When a memory segment becomes relevant, its assistant reasons within that context before passing along evidence. The master then aggregates these contributions. This makes memory access an active reasoning process, with local context informing what evidence is extracted.

On the LoCoMo benchmark, E-mem achieves an F1 score above 54%. The authors report that it surpasses GAM by 7.75% while reducing token cost by more than 70%. These results suggest that keeping contextual information available to specialized assistants can support stronger memory use while reducing the token expenditure reported in the evaluation.
icml-2026-e-mem-multi-agent-based-episod.tldr: E-mem uses assistants that reason over uncompressed memories, improving LoCoMo performance while reporting over 70% lower token cost.

paragraphs: Recognizing facial expressions in video requires following how expressions change over time. Changes in the surrounding scenario can distort these trajectories, making expression dynamics harder to interpret. EmWorld explicitly models both evolving scenarios and latent emotion states, addressing a gap in approaches that primarily align features or incrementally adapt to new domains.

The framework treats recognition as progressive Bayesian inference at two temporal scales. Its slow component uses stochastic evolutionary priors to track longer-term scenario changes and guide processing in new scenarios. Its fast component tracks expression changes between frames through temporally consistent latent transitions. Joint inference across these components aims to separate expression dynamics from the influence of the scenario.

Experiments on FERV39k, DFEW, and MAFW show consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods, with reported gains of up to 3.84%. The authors also report strong stability across scenarios and long-term robustness. These findings support explicitly tracking changing latent states as a useful approach to facial-expression recognition under evolving conditions.
icml-2026-emworld-emotion-world-model-wi.tldr: EmWorld jointly tracks slow scenario changes and fast expression dynamics to improve facial-expression recognition across evolving scenarios.

paragraphs: A time-series classifier can appear trustworthy when its explanations remain temporally consistent. This paper shows why that signal can be misleading: an adversarial change can alter the predicted class while preserving an explanation that looks plausible and agrees with a chosen reference rationale. Stable explanations therefore do not, by themselves, establish robust decisions.

The proposed Time Series Explanation Fooler, or TSEF, attacks two outputs jointly. It aims to induce a particular misclassification while keeping the explainer's output aligned with the reference. This differs from attacks concerned only with changing predictions, which can also disrupt explanations and spread attribution broadly. TSEF makes the separation between prediction behavior and explanation behavior an explicit objective.

Across multiple datasets and explanation backbones, the experiments consistently demonstrate this vulnerability. The implication is that evaluation should examine how explanations and decisions behave together under attack. The results establish that explanation stability can coexist with targeted prediction failure, motivating robustness checks that assess their coupling rather than interpreting consistency alone as reassurance.
icml-2026-exposing-vulnerabilities-in-ex.tldr: TSEF induces targeted time-series misclassifications while preserving reference-consistent explanations, showing that explanation stability can conceal decision failures.

paragraphs: Fleet addresses the difficulty of detecting images from rapidly changing generators. Detectors trained to recognize fixed artifacts can perform strongly on established benchmarks yet deteriorate against newer systems. The paper proposes continuous adaptation from a small number of examples as a response to this gap between benchmark success and changing real-world inputs.

Its adaptation mechanism constrains routing changes within separated feature subspaces. Specifically, avoidance routing redirects new AI-generated examples away from routes dominated by non-AI images. This focuses the update on how unfamiliar examples pass through the representation, replacing unconstrained feature changes. The authors also introduce Treasure, a benchmark containing 360,000 images from 64 models, including 20 closed-source commercial engines.

The experiments report severe failures for static state-of-the-art detectors on modern generators. For Doubao Seedream 4.0, Fleet raises the reported performance from 20.4% to 73.1% using ten adaptation examples. This result supports few-shot updates as a practical direction for handling emerging generators; it specifically demonstrates adaptation using new examples rather than universal zero-shot detection.
icml-2026-fleet-few-shots-lead-effective.tldr: Fleet adapts AI-image detection through constrained routing updates, substantially improving reported performance on a new generator with ten examples.

paragraphs: Satellite video tracking must follow targets amid changing backgrounds while processing high-resolution video with limited onboard computation. Fast correlation-filter trackers sacrifice accuracy, while stronger vision-transformer trackers can be too computationally demanding. FATrack aims to combine precise tracking with the speed needed for real-time satellite use.

Its lightweight transformer backbone routes tokens according to their relevance to the foreground target, concentrating computation on useful regions and suppressing redundant processing. Sparsifying tokens can damage the information and spatial relationships needed for tracking. FATrack therefore adds an Adaptive Scatter Module, which reinforces informative tokens using joint spatial-channel attention and sparse structural propagation to preserve semantic content and spatial coherence.

Across multiple satellite video benchmarks, FATrack exceeds existing real-time trackers in accuracy while achieving inference efficiency comparable to correlation-filter methods. The results support pairing selective computation with a mechanism that maintains information quality after sparsification. The paper presents this balance as evidence of potential for practical aerial tracking deployment, with the demonstrated performance grounded in its benchmark evaluations.
icml-2026-foreground-aware-token-routing.tldr: FATrack concentrates transformer computation on target-relevant regions while reinforcing sparse features to deliver accurate real-time satellite tracking.

paragraphs: Agents completing long tasks often receive a reward only at the end, making it difficult to determine which earlier actions deserve credit. This paper identifies an additional learning issue: policy-gradient magnitudes are coupled to uncertainty, measured through entropy. Confident correct actions can receive weak updates, while uncertain actions can produce large updates that destabilize learning.

Entropy-Modulated Policy Gradients recalibrates the learning signal using uncertainty at each step together with the final outcome. It strengthens updates for confident correct actions, penalizes confident mistakes, and reduces updates from uncertain steps to stabilize exploration. A further bonus rewards future clarity, encouraging the agent to pursue solution paths that become more predictable as it proceeds.

The framework is evaluated on WebShop, ALFWorld, and Deep Search, where it produces substantial gains over strong policy-gradient baselines. These findings support adjusting how outcome-based feedback is distributed through the learning update. The contribution concerns the interaction between confidence and update strength, extending efforts that primarily focus on supplying denser intermediate rewards.
icml-2026-harnessing-uncertainty-entropy.tldr: EMPG adjusts learning updates using stepwise uncertainty and final outcomes, improving long-horizon agents across three evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: Generating several possible solutions can improve language-model reasoning, but the system still needs to choose among them. This paper studies whether the way confidence changes during a solution provides useful evidence for that choice. Its central observation concerns the trajectory of confidence, rather than confidence treated as a single fixed property of an answer.

The authors find that correct reasoning traces tend to become more confident as they progress. Incorrect traces tend to show weaker confidence growth or declining confidence. Based on this pattern, they propose Confidence Dynamic Gain voting, which incorporates confidence evolution along the reasoning chain into answer selection. The paper also provides theoretical insights into the observed phenomenon.

Experiments cover DeepSeek-R1, gpt-oss, Gemma-3, and Qwen-QwQ on AIME24/25, HMMT25, and BRUMO25. The method significantly improves performance over the evaluated baselines. These results support confidence change as a useful discriminative signal across those settings. The observed tendency supplies evidence for ranking answers; it does not establish that every increasingly confident trace is correct.
icml-2026-inference-time-optimization-wi.tldr: Confidence Dynamic Gain voting improves answer selection by using the tendency of correct reasoning traces to gain confidence over time.

paragraphs: LakeQA tests question answering when finding the right evidence is itself a substantial part of the problem. Many reading-based evaluations provide relevant material or make it easy to retrieve. This benchmark instead places useful information inside a large, heterogeneous data collection, requiring agents to search before they can assemble an answer.

The collection contains 9.5 TB of text resources from Wikipedia and open-source government data, including structured and unstructured material. Each task is annotated by at least one Ph.D.-level expert. Questions require extended reasoning across multiple steps, but the intermediate steps are implicit: agents must identify relevant documents and combine evidence across sources without having the full route supplied.

Evaluation of seven frontier language models shows that the benchmark remains challenging. GPT-5.2, for example, achieves an exact-match score of 14.73%. This result reflects performance on a task that combines evidence discovery and reasoning. LakeQA provides a way to evaluate the complete process of locating and analyzing information in a large data lake.
icml-2026-lakeqa-an-exploratory-qa-bench.tldr: LakeQA evaluates agents on finding and combining evidence across a 9.5 TB data lake, exposing substantial challenges for tested frontier models.

paragraphs: This paper studies how to locate parts of a 3D object that support an action described through text or an interaction image. Its starting point is that an action depends on local physical attributes: a handle supports grasping because of properties such as curvature and thickness. Matching overall appearance can overlook these more specific relationships.

The proposed Attribute-Affordance Hierarchies framework explicitly connects region attributes to the actions they support. It first uses a hypergraph to capture relationships among local regions, then maps region-level concepts into hyperbolic space to represent their hierarchical organization. Counterfactual attribute samples encourage the model to learn dependencies that remain robust as attribute conditions vary.

By combining visual region structure with a hierarchy of concepts, the method seeks to identify where an affordance actually resides on an object. Experiments and qualitative analyses report improved localization and support the framework's effectiveness. The contribution is a more explicit account of how compositions of local attributes relate to actionable object regions in open-vocabulary grounding.
icml-2026-learning-attributeaffordance-h.tldr: Attribute-Affordance Hierarchies models how local object properties support actions, improving localization of actionable regions on 3D objects.

paragraphs: Adapting a language model to a specialized domain is difficult when little domain-specific training data exists. This paper investigates whether general-domain reasoning examples can help because they share question-answer structures and reasoning patterns with specialized tasks. Initial experiments find useful auxiliary signals even in general chain-of-thought data that has not been carefully selected.

NTK-Selector then aims to identify the most beneficial examples systematically. It draws on the Neural Tangent Kernel as a way to capture alignment in training dynamics. Because direct application to pretrained language models is impractical, the authors introduce a Jacobian-free approximation and empirically observe stable NTK-like behavior during fine-tuning. Selection is therefore motivated by how examples relate through learning dynamics.

Across medical, financial, legal, and psychological domains, NTK-Selector consistently outperforms domain-only fine-tuning and existing selection baselines. Reported gains are 8.7 points for Llama3-8B-Instruct and 5.1 for Qwen3-8B, compared with 0.8 and 0.9 from domain-only fine-tuning. The findings support mining general reasoning data as a useful supplement when specialized examples are scarce.
icml-2026-mining-useful-general-data-for.tldr: NTK-Selector mines general reasoning examples that improve specialized-domain adaptation when domain-specific training data is scarce.

paragraphs: Muon updates matrix parameters using the matrix sign of the gradient. This paper studies why that operation can help in a linear associative-memory model with softmax retrieval, where query-answer pairs occur at different frequencies. In this setting, ordinary gradient descent learns frequency components unevenly, allowing rare components to become a bottleneck.

The analysis shows that Muon reduces this imbalance and makes learning progress more uniform. Without label noise, the authors establish an exponential speedup over gradient descent in the studied model. With label noise and a power-law frequency spectrum, they derive a scaling law showing better scaling efficiency. These theoretical claims depend on the specified learning setting and frequency assumptions.

The authors interpret Muon as an implicit matrix preconditioner arising from adaptive task alignment and a block-symmetric gradient structure. A coordinate-wise sign preconditioner could match it with oracle access to unknown task representations, an access unavailable to practical SignGD. Synthetic long-tail classification and LLaMA-style pretraining experiments corroborate the theory, connecting the analytical explanation to empirical training behavior.
icml-2026-muon-in-associative-memory-lea.tldr: In a structured associative-memory model, Muon balances learning across frequency components and achieves stronger convergence and scaling than gradient descent.

paragraphs: Removing unwanted content from a text-to-image diffusion model must also preserve its useful generation abilities. This paper identifies two obstacles: training objectives that only indirectly represent the desired removal, and preservation constraints that overlook the model's underlying generative dynamics. The latter can allow broad forgetting while the model is being edited.

POSDA addresses both within one framework. It expresses unlearning as preference optimization, using a reward designed to directly quantify the removal objective. It also aligns distributions at the score level to preserve the topology of the model's underlying generative structure and prevent distributional drift. This makes preservation part of how the generative process is constrained, beyond restrictions on parameters or final outputs.

Experiments cover removing objects, styles, and NSFW content. The authors report state-of-the-art erasure effectiveness together with stronger retained utility than existing methods. These results support combining a more directly targeted unlearning objective with preservation of diffusion structure, allowing the evaluated models to remove unwanted concepts while maintaining more of their useful behavior.
icml-2026-preference-calibrated-optimiza.tldr: POSDA combines preference-based content removal with score-level distribution alignment to improve diffusion-model unlearning while preserving utility.

paragraphs: Alignment methods often optimize a preference-based reward while penalizing departures from the base language model through KL regularization. This paper argues that the penalty can preserve base-model biases that conflict with user preferences. Increasing rewards for preferred outputs can counter that influence, but it also raises the risk of exploiting imperfections in the reward model.

The authors formulate reward-model design as a Stackelberg game, representing the interaction between the chosen reward and the policy optimized under it. This shifts attention to how a reward should be shaped given the regularization imposed on the policy. They show that a simple shaping scheme can effectively approximate the optimal reward model in their formulation.

Empirical evaluation focuses on inference-time alignment. The method integrates into existing approaches with minimal overhead and consistently improves average reward. Its win–tie rates exceed 66% against every baseline when averaged across evaluation settings. These findings support accounting for the policy's regularization when designing rewards; the reported comparison combines wins and ties rather than measuring wins alone.
icml-2026-reward-shaping-for-inference-t.tldr: A game-theoretic reward-shaping method improves inference-time alignment by accounting for how KL regularization preserves base-policy biases.

paragraphs: Long visual sequences make vision-language inference expensive. This paper proposes deciding when visual information is needed by measuring its effect on predicted outputs. The motivation is that intermediate signals such as attention weights do not directly express whether retaining visual information changes what the model is about to say.

The training-free method constructs a prediction-conditioned Semantic Lens at fixed decoding intervals. It applies QR decomposition to the embeddings of the top candidate output tokens, producing an orthogonal semantic basis. Semantic Impact–Driven Visual Scheduling then projects visual-induced changes in hidden states onto that basis. This measurement guides dynamic scheduling of visual keys and values according to their relevance to current predictions.

The reported experiments achieve 87% visual KV compression while retaining more than 99% of model performance. These figures support using prediction-sensitive geometry to reduce visual information retained during inference. The result is specifically about compression and preserved evaluated performance; the framework's broader purpose is to make visual processing responsive to its changing contribution during generation.
icml-2026-semantic-impactdriven-visual-s.tldr: SIVS schedules visual keys and values by their impact on predictions, reporting 87% compression while retaining over 99% of model performance.

paragraphs: Reasoning models can spend unnecessary computation producing long chains of thought, even for simple questions. SuCo starts with Minimal Sufficient Chain of Thought: the shortest prefix of a reasoning trajectory that is adequate to produce the correct answer. The authors empirically find that using such prefixes can reduce reasoning tokens and improve accuracy across difficulty levels.

The framework trains continuous control of reasoning length in two stages. First, it constructs concise reasoning data using sufficiency thresholds that adapt to problem difficulty, then fine-tunes the model on these examples. Second, reinforcement learning tracks complexity dynamically and uses sufficiency-aware rewards to penalize both stopping too early and continuing unnecessarily.

Experiments across mathematics, programming, and science benchmarks show consistent gains in accuracy and reasoning efficiency. The approach makes sufficiency the organizing criterion for reasoning effort, extending beyond fixed budgets or a few discrete reasoning modes. Its findings support learning when enough reasoning has been done, while avoiding the assumption that simply shortening every reasoning trace will improve the answer.
icml-2026-suco-sufficiency-guided-contin.tldr: SuCo trains reasoning models to adapt their effort around sufficient reasoning, improving both accuracy and token efficiency in the evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: Language models exhibit both attention sinks, where attention concentrates on particular tokens, and unusually large activations. This paper revisits the idea that large activations are chiefly responsible for producing sink behavior. Its theoretical and empirical account instead assigns the two phenomena complementary roles in limiting excessive mixing of information between tokens.

In this account, attention sinks reduce mixing among tokens outside the sink, while massive activations reduce mixing between sink and non-sink tokens. The theory also explains how key-value biases, gating mechanisms, and normalization layers can eliminate massive activations while largely retaining attention sinks. This helps explain why the two phenomena can coexist without being inseparable.

Intervention experiments provide additional evidence: removing the sink token's value vector can restore attention sinks even when massive activations have been fully suppressed. The finding supports a mechanistic interpretation centered on information mixing within self-attention and normalization. It refines the relationship between the phenomena by showing how their functional roles can be distinguished through analysis and intervention.
icml-2026-towards-understanding-massive-.tldr: Theory and interventions suggest that attention sinks and massive activations play distinct, complementary roles in limiting token mixing.

paragraphs: Four-bit quantization can reduce language-model memory use and inference latency, but accuracy can suffer. Existing decomposition methods separate weights into a residual and a low-rank component, often handling outliers in the latter. TwinQuant identifies a mismatch: a decomposition that reduces real-valued residual energy need not minimize error after both components are quantized.

TwinQuant learns subspaces suited to quantization and jointly reshapes the residual and low-rank components. Component-specific transformations are optimized over Stiefel and general linear manifolds to flatten value distributions and reduce dynamic-range imbalance. The method therefore adapts the decomposition to the precision constraints that will actually apply during inference.

The authors also develop a fused kernel that pipelines low-rank computation on-chip and combines both components in a single final stage, avoiding intermediate global-memory traffic. Across LLaMA3 and Qwen3 models, TwinQuant retains accuracy close to FP16 and achieves up to 1.8 times end-to-end speedup over an FP16 baseline. The results connect quantization-aware representation design with an execution strategy that makes the decomposition efficient.
icml-2026-twinquant-learnable-subspace-d.tldr: TwinQuant learns quantization-friendly weight decompositions and uses a fused kernel to retain near-FP16 accuracy with up to 1.8× speedup.

paragraphs: Video reward models judge generated videos, but visual inputs consume substantial context and can become harder to use as reasoning continues. Packing all visual evidence into the initial prompt also limits how many frames can be included. VR-Thinker addresses these issues by allowing the model to actively acquire visual evidence during reasoning.

The model combines a visual reasoning operation with a configurable visual memory window. Training proceeds through three stages: curated visual reasoning traces teach the operation format; rejection sampling retains traces with correct judgments for further fine-tuning; and Group Relative Policy Optimization strengthens reasoning. This sequence develops both the ability to use visual operations and the reasoning needed to make preference judgments.

The seven-billion-parameter model achieves 80.5% accuracy on VideoGen Reward, 82.3% on GenAI-Bench, and 75.6% on MJ-Bench-Video. The authors report state-of-the-art accuracy among open-source models on these video preference benchmarks. The results support accessing visual evidence throughout reasoning as a useful way to improve the reliability of video reward judgments.
icml-2026-vr-thinker-boosting-video-rewa.tldr: VR-Thinker actively gathers visual evidence during reasoning and achieves leading reported open-source accuracy on video preference benchmarks.
